Any divergence should prompt suspicion of the estimates, and divergences that persist as the step size shrinks indicate bias that calls for reparameterisation (for example non-centred forms) or stronger priors. sources.citation: Johannes Bracher; Evan L. Ray; Tilmann Gneiting; Nicholas G. Reich (2021). Evaluating epidemic forecasts in an interval format. PLOS Computational Biology 17(2):e1008618
sources.note: Backs: When forecasts are issued as central intervals, the weighted interval score (WIS) combines the absolute error of the median with interval scores at K levels, using weights w0 = 1/2 and wk = alpha_k/2. It is proper for any non-negative weights, approximates the CRPS as K grows, generalises absolute error, and decomposes into a dispersion term plus over- and under-prediction penalties. The COVID-19 Forecast Hub scores the median plus K = 11 intervals (nominal 98%, 95%, 90%, ..., 10%). Inverse-U PIT histograms mark overdispersed forecasts.

sources.citation: Glenn W. Brier (1950). Verification of Forecasts Expressed in Terms of Probability. Monthly Weather Review 78(1):1-3
sources.checked: verified; the figures were corrected against the source
sources.note: Backs: Brier proposed scoring probability forecasts of a binary event by the mean squared difference between the stated probability and the 0/1 outcome (0 is perfect, lower is better). It is the standard verification score for yes/no events and is what the model uses for threshold passage and for the bloc-majority probability. Because it is an average over events, pooling many near-certain events (lists sure to pass) shrinks it without saying anything about the hard cases, so it needs a stratified or skill-score companion. Corrected against the source: Monthly Weather Review 78(1):1-3. Brier defined P = (1/n) sum_i sum_j (f_ij - E_ij)^2 over all r classes (0 perfect, 2 worst); for a binary event twice the one-component (p - o)^2 score now called the Brier score (per secondary sources; original scan not opened).

sources.note: Backs: For time series, leave-one-out cross-validation lets future observations inform predictions of the past, so it is over-optimistic as a measure of forecasting skill. Leave-future-out cross-validation respects time order, and Pareto-smoothed importance sampling can approximate it without one refit per step.

The belief that pseudo-out-of-sample analysis is the best insurance against in-sample overfitting in model comparison is largely false, and in finite samples it widens the scope for data mining (for example over the choice of sample split). Its legitimate use is learning about comparative historical predictive performance.

sources.note: Backs: A Bayesian workflow validates computation with fake-data simulation (refitting data simulated from known parameters) and, more thoroughly, with simulation-based calibration, which needs many refits. It also warns that picking one model from many similar ones by minimising cross-validation error overfits and gives suboptimal choices, and recommends projection-predictive selection or stacking instead.

sources.citation: Tilmann Gneiting (2011). Making and Evaluating Point Forecasts. Journal of the American Statistical Association 106(494):746-762
sources.note: Backs: Point forecasts are meaningful only when the scoring function is fixed in advance, or the forecaster is told which functional (mean, median, quantile) to report, and the scoring function must be consistent for that functional. Mismatches can produce grossly misguided comparisons. Quantiles, including the median, are elicited by generalised piecewise-linear scores such as absolute error; means are elicited by Bregman scores such as squared error.

sources.citation: Tilmann Gneiting; Fadoua Balabdaoui; Adrian E. Raftery (2007). Probabilistic forecasts, calibration and sharpness. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B 69(2):243-268
sources.note: Backs: Probabilistic forecasts should maximise sharpness subject to calibration. Calibration (statistical consistency between forecasts and outcomes) comes first, and among calibrated forecasts the sharper one is better. A hump-shaped PIT or rank histogram signals overdispersed forecasts whose prediction intervals are too wide on average, and sharpness is read from the average width of the central 50% and 90% intervals. Over-coverage is therefore a calibration failure, not a safety margin.

sources.citation: Matthew D. Hoffman; Andrew Gelman (2014). The No-U-Turn Sampler: Adaptively Setting Path Lengths in Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. Journal of Machine Learning Research 15(47):1593-1623
sources.note: Backs: The No-U-Turn Sampler removes Hamiltonian Monte Carlo's hand-tuned path length by extending trajectories until they begin to double back, and adapts the step size by dual averaging. It performs at least as efficiently as well-tuned HMC without costly tuning runs.

sources.citation: Benjamin E. Lauderdale; Drew Linzer (2015). Under-performing, over-performing, or just performing? The limitations of fundamentals-based presidential election forecasting. International Journal of Forecasting 31(3):965-979
sources.note: Backs: Election forecasts built on a few historical elections usually overstate their certainty, because they ignore uncertainty in coefficient estimates and in specification choices; with limited data, many models are empirically justifiable. Once those sources were accounted for, 95% intervals widened to about +/-10 points of vote share at the state level and +/-7 nationally.

sources.citation: Brian A. Nosek; Charles R. Ebersole; Alexander C. DeHaven; David T. Mellor (2018). The preregistration revolution. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 115(11):2600-2606
sources.note: Backs: Pre-registration, which fixes the questions and the analysis plan before the outcomes are seen, separates testing predictions from generating postdictions, a line that hindsight bias otherwise blurs. Partial strategies keep it usable when the data already exist.

sources.note: Backs: When data have temporal, spatial or hierarchical structure, random cross-validation seriously underestimates predictive error. Folds should be blocked on the dependence structure, even when fitted residuals look uncorrelated, though blocking can force extrapolation and so overstate error.

sources.note: Backs: Few proper scores exist for multivariate forecasts. The energy score is the usual choice for sample (ensemble) forecasts but has limited power to detect a wrongly specified correlation between components. Variogram-based scores, built from pairwise differences between components, were distinctly more sensitive to errors in the correlation structure in simulations and in a five-site wind case study. They are proper but not strictly proper, so the authors use them alongside other scores.

Calibration alone is not skill: giving every NCAA team a 1-in-68 chance is calibrated and useless, so FiveThirtyEight also reports Brier skill scores. Its election forecasts have historically leaned underconfident. Corrected against the source: FiveThirtyEight, 4 Apr 2019: of 5,589 events forecast at 70%, 71% happened; of 55,853 near 5%, 4% happened; candidates given 75% won 83% (generally not statistically significant).

sources.citation: Sudhir Varma; Richard Simon (2006). Bias in error estimation when using cross-validation for model selection. BMC Bioinformatics 7:91
sources.note: Backs: When cross-validation is used both to tune a model and to report its error, the reported error is substantially optimistic. On null datasets with no real signal, tuned classifiers showed low CV error while their independent-test performance was at chance. Nested CV (tuning inside an inner loop, error estimated in an outer loop) was nearly unbiased, so every selection step must be repeated inside each fold.

sources.citation: Aki Vehtari; Andrew Gelman; Jonah Gabry (2017). Practical Bayesian model evaluation using leave-one-out cross-validation and WAIC. Statistics and Computing 27(5):1413-1432
sources.note: Backs: Leave-one-out cross-validation estimates pointwise out-of-sample predictive accuracy. Computed per held-out unit, it also gives approximate standard errors for each model's predictive error and for the difference between two models, which should accompany any comparison.

sources.citation: Aki Vehtari; Andrew Gelman; Daniel Simpson; Bob Carpenter; Paul-Christian Burkner (2021). Rank-Normalization, Folding, and Localization: An Improved R-hat for Assessing Convergence of MCMC. Bayesian Analysis 16(2):667-718 (journal pagination not re-checked this session)
sources.checked: verified; the figures were corrected against the source
sources.note: Backs: Rank-normalised split-R-hat should be below 1.01 (the old 1.1 rule passes chains that have not converged), with at least four chains. Rank-normalised bulk ESS should exceed 400 for stable Monte Carlo standard errors. When intervals or quantiles are reported, the tail-ESS (at the 5% and 95% quantiles) must also be adequate, and the MCSE should be checked for every quantity of interest. Corrected against the source: Bayesian Analysis 16(2):667-718, doi 10.1214/20-BA1221; arXiv Sec. 2 pp. 4-5. sources.citation: Aki Vehtari; Daniel Simpson; Andrew Gelman; Yuling Yao; Jonah Gabry (2024). Pareto Smoothed Importance Sampling. Journal of Machine Learning Research 25(72):1-58
sources.note: Backs: Pareto-smoothed importance sampling stabilises importance weights, and its fitted Pareto shape k-hat is a reliability diagnostic. Estimates are trustworthy when k-hat < min(1 - 1/log10(S), 0.7). Above 0.7 they should not be trusted, and the affected leave-one-out folds should be refit exactly (PSIS-LOO+) or replaced by K-fold CV.

sources.citation: Sean Jeremy Westwood; Solomon Messing; Yphtach Lelkes (2020). Projecting Confidence: How the Probabilistic Horse Race Confuses and Demobilizes the Public. The Journal of Politics 82(4):1530-1544
sources.note: Backs: In survey experiments, people shown a win probability were more confident about who was ahead and who would win than people shown a vote-share projection with a margin of error, and participants in every format misjudged the chance of winning. In an incentivised voting game, higher win probabilities (but not larger vote-share leads) reduced paying to vote. Small vote-share leads map to large win probabilities, which readers misread.
